title: Biodiversity Register — Class 6 CBSE Vocational Education
subject: Vocational Education

slides.title: Biodiversity Register
bullets: Class 6 — CBSE Vocational Education
Kaushal Bodh — Chapter 2
slides.speaker_notes: Look closely at the world around you — you'll find more life than you expect.

slides.title: What you'll be able to do
bullets: Define biodiversity and its three levels.
Describe a register entry's structure.
Identify common habitats + their inhabitants.
Apply field-observation principles.
Use multiple sources of information.
Plan a 4-week project + share findings.

slides.title: What is biodiversity?
bullets: Bio (life) + diversity (variety).
The variety of life on Earth.
Three levels: SPECIES / GENETIC / ECOSYSTEM.
India is one of the most biodiverse countries.
~1 lakh known species in India.

slides.title: Three levels of biodiversity
bullets: SPECIES — different KINDS (mango vs neem).
GENETIC — different VARIETIES within a species (basmati vs sona masoori rice).
ECOSYSTEM — different KINDS OF PLACES (forest, river, desert).
Loss at any level reduces overall biodiversity.
Each level is studied differently.

slides.title: What is a biodiversity register?
bullets: A careful record of living things in a chosen area.
Made by people who live or visit there.
School register — campus + small radius.
Each entry: place, habitat, living thing, date, time, source.
People's Biodiversity Register — kept by panchayat BMCs.

slides.title: A sample register entry
bullets: Place — beside basketball court (under peepal tree).
Habitat — shaded ground with fallen leaves.
Living thing — small grey-brown bird with white cheeks.
Possibly: house sparrow (Passer domesticus).
Source: my observation, 14 Aug 2026, 7 a.m.

slides.title: Where to look — habitats
bullets: Trees and bushes — birds, lichens, insects.
Ground — ants, beetles, frogs after rain.
Soil — earthworms, microbes.
Walls and stones — gecko, spider, moss.
Water — tadpoles, algae; Air — butterflies, bees.

slides.title: When to look
bullets: Early morning — birds active.
Mid-morning to noon — many insects.
Late afternoon — some mammals come out.
After rain — snails, earthworms, frogs.
Visit each habitat at MULTIPLE times of day.

slides.title: How to observe — golden rules
bullets: Stay still and quiet for 2–3 minutes.
Sketch + describe colour, size, behaviour.
Record place, time and weather.
Honest uncertainty: 'possibly X'.
NEVER catch or hurt living things.

slides.title: Tools for the field
bullets: Small notebook + pencil (works in rain).
Magnifying glass for tiny insects/lichens.
Measuring tape for sizes.
Simple field guide of the region.
Camera or phone (with permission).

slides.title: Sources of information
bullets: Local people — farmers, elders, gardeners.
Field guides + library books.
Reliable websites — iNaturalist, India Biodiversity Portal.
School atlases + NCERT science textbooks.
Always RECORD your source.

slides.title: Why biodiversity matters
bullets: Bees pollinate brinjal and tomato.
Birds eat insects that would damage crops.
Earthworms make soil fertile.
Trees cool the playground in summer.
All these are FREE ecosystem services.

slides.title: Sharing your register
bullets: A POSTER — sketch + photos + notes.
A SLIDE DECK — one slide per habitat.
A SHORT TALK — three favourites, one minute each.
A HANDOUT — one-page list with pictures.
Raise NEW questions for the school.

slides.title: You try (5 min)
bullets: 1. Define biodiversity in one sentence.
2. Name the three levels.
3. List 3 habitats around your school.
4. Write one register entry for a sparrow.
5. Name 2 sources you would use to identify a tree.

slides.title: Quick check
bullets: Q1. SPECIES vs GENETIC diversity?
Q2. Best time to observe birds?
Q3. Pencil or pen in the field?
Q4. Honest uncertainty — what does it mean?
Show fingers.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Biodiversity = variety of life at species, genetic, ecosystem levels.
A register records what lives where, when and how — with a source.
Visit many habitats at different times.
Observe quietly; never catch or hurt; be honest about uncertainty.
Use local people, field guides and reliable websites.
Share via poster, slides or short talk; raise new questions.
Recording biodiversity is itself a small act of conservation.
